blocks.text: For anagram grouping, sorted characters or a frequency signature can be canonical keys. A lossy key merges records that should remain separate.

messages.text: Ignoring a defining field creates false groups.
One key collapses all records into one bucket.
Random keys prevent intended equal records from meeting.

feedback.reason: The key is a canonical representation of the grouping relation.

options.text: Equivalent records produce the same key, and records from different groups do not collide under the contract.
Every record receives a random key so no two records group together.
Only the first field is used even when other fields define equivalence.
One key is shared by every record.

prompt: What makes a grouping key safe for records that should be considered equivalent?

blocks.text: Initialize an empty bucket when the key first appears, then append each subsequent member. Replacement silently loses earlier group members.

messages.text: An existing key is evidence of a group, not a reason to remove it.
Unrelated keys must retain their own groups.
Replacement discards prior members.

feedback.reason: A bucket represents all members of the equivalence class.

options.text: Append the record to that key's bucket.
Replace the existing bucket with the new record only.
Delete the key because it already exists.
Move records from every other key into this bucket.

prompt: When a new record maps to an existing grouping key, what update preserves the full group?

blocks.text: Key design is part of correctness. Include every property that distinguishes groups, then normalize only properties the problem declares irrelevant.

messages.text: Construction cost and lookup complexity are separate from semantic collisions.
The omitted field can be decisive for equivalence.
Omission tends to merge distinct records rather than split equal ones.

feedback.reason: Different records with the same lossy projection share a key even when they should not be equivalent.

options.text: Distinct groups can collide and be merged into one bucket.
Equivalent records are guaranteed to separate into different buckets.
The key becomes constant-time regardless of its construction.
Omitted fields never affect grouping correctness.

prompt: What is the consequence of using a grouping key that omits a field required by the equivalence relation?

blocks.text: As with zero frequencies, removal is valid only when historical empty groups are not part of the output. The key's lifecycle must match the contract.

messages.text: Different keys must not be merged.
Retaining all empty buckets wastes state and can confuse active-group counts.
Nonempty buckets still represent valid group members.

feedback.reason: An empty bucket contributes no members and can be removed to keep active state compact.

options.text: When the bucket becomes empty, unless the contract explicitly needs empty group keys.
Remove it whenever it still contains members.
Never remove buckets, even when no member remains.
Merge empty buckets into the next key.

prompt: When should a grouping map remove a bucket after records are deleted?

blocks.text: The key decides equivalence, while the payload decides what information remains available after grouping. Appending each record to its bucket preserves the complete output. If the requirement later changes to a histogram, the bucket may be replaced by a count, but that is a different state contract.

messages.text: A count preserves group size but discards the record identities required by the output.
Presence can confirm that a group exists but cannot construct the group’s members.

feedback.reason: Materialized grouping requires a key-to-members bucket; presence and count are lossy aggregates.

options.text: A boolean indicating that the key has appeared.
A list or bucket containing the original records in that group.
Only the number of records assigned to the key.

prompt: The output must return each complete group of records. What should the map store under a canonical grouping key?

blocks.text: The key is not merely a convenient label—it defines the grouping relation implemented by the map. Sorting removes order while preserving every character and multiplicity. A frequency vector could represent the same relation under a fixed alphabet; shorter lossy summaries such as length or first character merge non-equivalent inputs.

messages.text: The first character is neither order-independent nor complete enough to represent the multiset of characters.
Equal length is necessary but not sufficient; unrelated strings of the same length would be merged.
Different permutations remain different keys, so equivalent strings would be split into separate buckets.

feedback.reason: A grouping key must be identical exactly for members of the intended equivalence class; sorted characters provide that canonical signature.

options.text: The original string unchanged.
Only the string length.
Only the first character.
The characters sorted into a canonical sequence.

prompt: Strings must be grouped when they contain the same characters with the same multiplicities, regardless of order. Which key correctly represents the equivalence relation?

blocks.text: “Check before insert” is not a universal hash rule. Grouping needs a bucket to receive the current record, so creating it on first use is the correct state transition. The decisive question is what membership means at the decision point: prior evidence in duplicate/pair checks, or initialized storage in grouping.

messages.text: An empty bucket and a populated bucket differ materially; the safety comes from the explicit initialization step followed by append, not from equivalence.
Operation order depends on the invariant. Insert-first is unsafe when membership is supposed to prove prior occurrence, such as self-pair-sensitive complement lookup.

feedback.reason: Here insertion establishes storage for the current member; it is not treated as proof that an earlier member existed.

options.text: Insertion before every possible check is always safe for hash algorithms.
An empty bucket and a populated bucket mean the same thing.
The new key is initialization for the current record; existence is not being used as evidence of a prior distinct record.

prompt: For grouping, the algorithm checks whether a bucket exists, creates an empty bucket if absent, and then appends the current record. Why is creating the bucket before the append safe?

blocks.text: The empty count tuple or empty sorted representation is a legitimate key. Skipping it loses input records; per-occurrence keys split an equivalence class; length-only keys merge all equal-length non-equivalent strings.

messages.text: Length does not capture character multiplicity or identity for nonempty records.
Equivalent empty strings must share a bucket.
Empty records still belong to an output group.

feedback.reason: Canonicalization must cover boundary records while preserving the required equivalence relation.

options.text: Every empty string maps to the same valid canonical signature, and that signature does not collide with a nonempty string.
Ignore empty strings because they have no characters to sort or count.
Assign a new key per empty occurrence so their buckets remain distinguishable.
Use only length for all strings because empty length is unique.

prompt: Several empty strings must be grouped with all other empty strings. What property should their canonical key have?

blocks.text: The grouping invariant assumes a stored key continues to denote the same equivalence class. Reusing and mutating the same object can make previously inserted state no longer correspond to the original record or can produce identity-based keys. An immutable tuple, string encoding, or copied value preserves key stability.

messages.text: Mutating key state after insertion can change its semantic meaning or use object identity rather than the intended count values, depending on the language.
The signature length is fixed and contains none of the per-character counts that define the group.

feedback.reason: A map key must remain a stable canonical representation of one record’s equivalence signature.

options.text: Insert the mutable list itself and then modify it for the next record.
Replace the signature with the number of entries.
Convert the current counts into an immutable canonical value or copied encoding.

prompt: A grouping signature is built from a mutable list of counts that will be reused for the next record. What must happen before using it as a map key?

blocks.text: A canonical signature such as sorted characters or a count tuple can represent the intended class. If a compact hash is used, equality verification or collision-resistant contract is required before merging records. Length and hash equality alone are not semantic equality.

messages.text: Merging unequal records changes the required groups.
Hash collisions are possible unless the representation is defined as a full canonical key.
Many unequal records have the same length.

feedback.reason: Grouping keys must preserve equivalence semantics; a hash value alone may collide for unequal records.

options.text: The key must be a collision-free representation of the required equivalence relation, or collisions must be resolved without merging unequal records.
Equal hash codes always prove the records belong to the same group.
Equal record length is sufficient for grouping.
Every key collision is acceptable because grouping never observes record identity.

prompt: Two records map to the same grouping key. What must be true before placing them in the same output bucket?

blocks.text: Normalization is part of the grouping definition. Under-normalization splits equivalent records; over-normalization merges distinct ones. The key should therefore trim and case-fold while retaining punctuation. This rule transfers to composite business keys, locale-aware text, and normalized identifiers only when every transformation is explicitly justified.

messages.text: Length is a lossy summary and merges unrelated normalized codes.
Raw casing and surrounding spaces would split records that the contract declares equivalent.
Removing punctuation changes the stated equivalence relation and can merge codes that must remain distinct.

feedback.reason: The canonical key must apply exactly the equivalence transformations in the contract—no fewer and no more.

options.text: Trim, lower-case, and remove all punctuation.
Use the raw code without normalization.
Use only the normalized code length.
Trim surrounding spaces and apply a documented case-folding normalization, preserving punctuation.

prompt: Customer codes must be grouped after trimming surrounding spaces and ignoring letter case, while punctuation remains significant. Which key is valid?

blocks.text: A valid grouping key must implement the intended equivalence relation, not merely correlate with it. Sorted strings and fixed-position count vectors are injective over character multisets in the stated alphabet. This decision is separate from the hash table’s own collision handling: the semantic key itself must not deliberately merge unequal classes.

messages.text: Length preserves only total multiplicity and merges every same-length string regardless of character composition.
Different character multisets can have the same code sum, so this key creates semantic collisions even before hash-table collisions are considered.
Omitting count_vector misses a complete fixed-alphabet signature whose positions identify characters and values identify multiplicities.
Omitting sorted_string misses a complete canonical representation that preserves every character and multiplicity while removing order.

feedback.reason: Both a sorted sequence and a canonical count vector encode the full multiset; sums and lengths are lossy summaries.

options.text: The sorted string.
The sum of character code values.
A 26-entry vector of character counts encoded canonically.
The string length.

prompt: Assume lowercase English letters only. Select all keys that can exactly group strings by character multiset.

blocks.text: Set and map keys may have the same equality semantics, yet their information contracts differ. Replacing a grouping map with a set is safe only if the output no longer needs members, counts, or aggregates. This is a common mismatch because both structures appear to “organize by key,” but only the map preserves a payload.

messages.text: Deduplicating keys is exactly what a set continues to do.
A set still supports key membership and can detect that a category already exists.

feedback.reason: The set retains group existence but removes the association from each key to its members.

options.text: Detecting whether a grouping key has appeared.
Reconstructing which original records belong to each group.
Keeping only one instance of each grouping key.

prompt: A developer replaces a key-to-record-list map with a set of canonical keys. Which capability is lost?

constraints: Assume each key is materialized from all m characters.
Count retained canonical keys and bucketed string content as extra space for this item.

blocks.text: Sorting one length-m string costs O(m log m); repeating it for n strings costs n · O(m log m) = O(nm log m). Materializing or hashing each m-character key and performing n expected-constant bucket operations adds at most O(nm), which does not exceed the sorting term.

items: Time O(n) ignores work across m characters per string, while O(nm) counts only linear key reading and omits sorting each key.
Time O(n log n) sorts n records rather than the m characters inside each record, and O(n²m) invents pairwise record processing that the grouping loop does not perform.
The retained canonical keys and bucket contents contain Θ(nm) characters under the stated convention, so O(1), O(n), and O(m) each omit one growing dimension.
Space O(nm log m) incorrectly carries the sorting-time logarithm into retained storage; no logarithmic number of copies is kept.

blocks.text: This item explicitly counts retained keys and returned bucket contents as extra space. Under a convention that reports required output separately, the same Θ(nm) materialized result would be labeled output space instead.
blocks.title: Accounting convention

feedback.reason: Key construction dominates with a sort per string, while retaining all grouped content requires space proportional to total input size.

prompt: n strings each have length m. For each string, the algorithm sorts its characters to form a grouping key and then performs one expected O(1) hash-map bucket update. Classify expected time and extra space when the output buckets retain all input characters.
